title: Mind first
hook: spending too long on the body is a sign of neglecting the mind (Enchiridion 41)

segments.voice: Yesterday: praise that teaches people what they're worth. Your line was honor the character. Whose character did you name out loud? Day three hundred seventy-six.

Add it up for one ordinary day. The workout. The shower and the hair. The meals, the snacks, the planning of meals. The skincare, the mirror, the step count on the watch. Now add up the minutes that went to the mind on purpose: thinking something through, reading something that stretched you, asking whether a judgment was true. Which list is longer? Epictetus doesn't ask you to drop the first one. He asks you to look at the ratio. Today: mind first.
screen: `ADD UP THE BODY'S MINUTES.` → `NOW THE MIND'S.` → `MIND FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the line. It's a sign of a dull nature, Epictetus says, to spend a lot of time on the things of the body: a lot of exercise, a lot of eating, a lot of drinking, and the rest of the body's business. Second, the key word is a lot. He isn't against the body. His own teacher, Musonius Rufus, taught that students should train the body as well as the soul, through cold and heat and hard work. Epictetus doesn't forbid eating, drinking or exercise either. He asks you to notice when the body's business takes up the whole day. These things, he says, should be done in passing, along the way. Third, where the attention goes instead. All your care, he says, should turn toward the mind. The Greek here is gnōmē, a word for judgment, outlook, the way a person thinks things through. For the Stoics, that's where a life actually gets lived: in how you judge what happens. A well-tended body with a neglected mind is like a beautifully kept house where no one ever opens the windows. Fourth, why it's urgent and not just nice. The body will be looked after whether you plan it or not. Hunger reminds you. Tiredness reminds you. Nothing in the day reminds you to think. The mind only gets its turn if you give it one on purpose. That's why the handbook tilts so hard in one direction. Not because the body doesn't matter, but because the mind is the one that gets forgotten.
screen: `TOO MUCH TIME ON THE BODY.` · `DO THE BODY'S THINGS IN PASSING.` · `GNŌMĒ: TURN YOUR CARE TO THE MIND.` · `NOTHING REMINDS YOU TO THINK.` · then, large: `MIND FIRST.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the body be looked after for a minute: let it sit, let it breathe. Now give the mind its turn. Pick one question that deserves real thought. Something you believe and have never checked. A decision you keep putting off. A line from this handbook that bothered you. Turn it over slowly, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. No need to answer it. Just think on purpose. The bell holds the time.
Mind first. Enchiridion forty-one: do the body's business in passing, and turn your real care toward the mind. Today's word.
Your line: mind first. Give five minutes to the mind today on purpose: a page that stretches you, or one question thought all the way through. Day three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism keep the body's routines simple and set aside a few deliberate minutes each day for reading, reflection or journaling.

fork.setup: you have a free half hour. you've already worked out and planned dinner. what does Enchiridion 41 point to?
options: give the time to the mind: read, or think something through.
fork.reveal: the body's business in passing, he says, and all your care toward the mind.

original.note: Greek: judgment, outlook, mind, where Enchiridion 41 says to turn all your care.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoics thought the body didn't matter.
what it means: look after the body in passing, and give the mind deliberate attention, since nothing else will remind you to.
what a scholar hears: gnōmē, judgment or outlook; his teacher Musonius trained the body too, so the target is 'a lot', not the body.

notes: Enchiridion 41 paraphrased: a sign of a dull disposition to occupy oneself much with the body: much exercise, eating, drinking, evacuation, copulation; these should be done incidentally; all attention to the mind. The last two items are softened to 'the rest of the body's business'. Confirm.
Greek γνώμη as the word in Ench. 41 ('περὶ δὲ τὴν γνώμην ἡ πᾶσα ἔστω ἐπιστροφή'): confirm before keeping the original game.
Musonius Rufus, Lecture 6: training of both soul and body (cold, heat, hardship). Confirm.
